Q1.answer: When several LLM agents share a memory, a system must decide whose memory to consult per query. Consulting all agents (global search) costs tokens on every query. The paper measures how much routing each query to a learned topic owner (ASMOS) saves in LLM tokens, what it costs in accuracy, and how routing adapts to a new topic.

Q2.answer: Global search spends LLM tokens on every query, so narrowing whom to ask could lower per-query cost. The paper asserts this cost matters but gives no absolute scale beyond 39.8 of 180.2 tokens per query, and does not measure scaling with team or memory size.
Q2.missing: Why a saving of about 40 tokens per query matters in practice (deployment scale, cost at larger teams) is not argued.

Q3.answer: The paper frames the gap as one of measurement: what learned ownership saves relative to global search, what it costs in answer quality, and how it behaves when topics change. It explicitly cannot say what existing routing or memory methods lack, because no literature search was run.
Q3.missing: No related work is cited; the shortcoming of existing approaches is not identified.

Q4.answer: They compared four routing arms on 50 queries over a deliberately constructed two-agent corpus with gpt-4o-mini and 10 seeds: global search (A0), learned-ownership routing (A1, ASMOS), ownership frozen at prior (A2), and similarity-only routing (A3), measuring LLM tokens per query, accuracy, answerability and route@1. They also ran new-topic adaptation runs against frozen and periodically retrained classifier routers with two embedders, a single stationary embedder run, and a one-run static QA comparison of No-Memory, RAG, ASMOS-memory and ASMOS+RAG.

Q5.answer: ASMOS itself is taken as given (the paper measures it rather than proposing it). The statistical choices are justified: bootstrap CI over queries; Wilcoxon signed-rank with zeros dropped to keep a stated pre-registered p-value; rank-biserial correlation because it pairs with the signed-rank test and has one definition; n_eff reported to avoid misreading r. Why ownership-based routing should save tokens is only implied (it narrows candidates).
Q5.missing: No rationale for the ownership-routing design itself or for choosing the specific baselines beyond availability.

Q6.answer: (1) Cost experiment: 4 arms, 50 queries, gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0, 10 seeds (only 5 with accuracy etc.), threshold 0.351493. (2) Frozen-ownership ablation (A2). (3) New-topic adaptation: 10 steps x 5 queries x 5 seeds, all-mpnet-base-v2 and bge-m3, vs classifier frozen/retrained every 5/10 steps, measured by cumulative regret in route@1. (4) Single stationary run with MiniLM-L6-v2 and hash fallback. (5) Static QA on 24 items from RULER, one run, four systems. Plus signed-rank statistics for other answering models in Appendix A.

Q7.answer: A1 used 22.1% fewer LLM tokens per query than global search (180.2 vs 140.4; bootstrap 95% CI 17.9% to 26.3%; Wilcoxon p = 6.8e-09, r = 0.941 over 48 non-zero pairs; per-seed 21.9-22.2%), with equal answerability 0.98. In new-topic runs ASMOS had regret 3.24 (mpnet) and 0.92 (bge-m3) with no retraining vs 4.8, 9.0 and 10.0 for classifiers.

Q8.answer: On this constructed two-agent corpus with gpt-4o-mini, routing to a learned owner reliably reduces recorded LLM tokens per query by roughly a fifth relative to global search; the frozen-ownership arm, which does not route, loses the saving, consistent with the saving requiring routing; and in the tested new-topic runs ASMOS reached the new owner without retraining (while using as many labels).

Q9.answer: They do not establish the saving on organic workloads, larger teams or other answering models; a whole-system net saving (embedding, verification, ownership updates excluded); the size or reliability of the accuracy drop; that the learning process (vs any correct static ownership) causes the saving; a statistically supported or fairly matched adaptation advantage over classifiers (untested, not matched on tuning/update access, no online classifier); faster or more sample-efficient learning; any benefit of ASMOS-memory for QA.

Q10.answer: A bounded measurement: a 22.1% per-query LLM token saving of learned-ownership routing over global search with a properly reported uncertainty (CI, signed-rank test, effect size with n_eff), accompanied by an honest accounting of lower accuracy and of what the ablation and adaptation runs can and cannot show.

Q11.answer: Constructed corpus with two agents; one answering model for the headline; seeds 11-55 from an absent file and near-identical seeds; embedder unrecorded for the cost run; undocumented method pieces (claims, verification, topics, update rule, prior, candidates), accuracy grading, answerability definition and query classes; untested accuracy difference; ablation cannot isolate learning; unmatched and untested adaptation comparison; threshold tuned in-corpus; token measure excludes embedding, verification and ownership updates; static QA is one run of 24 items with inconsistent metrics; no literature positioning; corpus and code unavailable.

Q12.answer: On a constructed two-agent corpus, routing queries to a learned topic owner cut LLM tokens per query by about 22% versus asking everyone, at a small but unbounded accuracy cost; it is a cost/routing tool, not a QA-quality method, and much of the method and evaluation is undocumented.
